newsitem.title: UK: Obese cousins point to human fat gene - reports.
newsitem.headline: Obese cousins point to human fat gene - reports.

text.p: A pair of obese cousins offer the first evidence of a specific genetic mutation that can be blamed for obesity in people, British researchers reported on Monday.
They found a second mutation in an overweight woman, indicating that a number of genes may be implicated.
The cousins, a girl aged eight and boy of two, have the same mutation in the gene that orders the body to produce leptin, a newly discovered hormone linked with body fat.

Sadaf Farooqi and colleagues at Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge, writing in the science journal Nature, said that despite considerable evidence that genetic factors contribute to obesity, no actual human genetic mutation had previously been singled.
But the case of the two fat young cousins offered new clues. They belong to a highly interbred family -- their parents are first cousins, as were their grandparents.
"Although of normal weight at birth, both children suffered from severe, intractable obesity from an early age," Farooqi's group wrote.
Each child has two siblings of normal weight, although plump, and none of their parents are clinically obese.
The eight-year-old weighs 86 kg (190 pounds) and could hardly walk because she had so much body fat. Liposuction on her legs helped somewhat, Farooqi said.
The two-year-old weighs 29 kg (64 pounds) and more than half his body weight is fat. Both children ate ravenously and constantly from the time they were babies.
Farooqi's group found a single mutation in the gene for leptin in both children. Checks showed both sets of parents carried one copy of the mutated gene while the children had two copies each.
The children produce very little or no leptin, Farooqi said.
Leptin was first found in 1994 in mice. It is secreted by fat cells.
Obese mice given leptin lose weight and other symptoms associated with obesity, such as an inability to process sugars properly, are reduced.
Researchers think leptin acts on cells in the hypothalamus, the body's central hormonal control centre, located in the base of the brain.

It is probably one of the signallers that tells the body it has had enough to eat. Some obese people have too much leptin -- which may mean their body is insensitive to its effects, while others have too little.
Farooqi stressed that the children's' condition was extremely rare.
"Leptin mutations are unlikely to be a cause in the majority of people with obesity," she said in a telephone interview.
"But it does show that leptin has an important role to play in humans."

Members of the same research team said they had identified mutations in a gene for an enzyme that helps process hormones known as prohormone convertase (PC1) in a woman who was severely obese as a child. She had been put on a strict diet and was now mildly obese.
PC1 helps in the processing of insulin and other hormones implicated in weight control.
This woman had normal leptin levels, Robert Jackson of Addenbrooke's and colleagues wrote in the journal Nature Genetics.
Rudolph Leibel of the Rockefeller University in New York said genes were probably to blame in up to 80 percent of obesity cases.
"However, until now, no instance of human obesity has been proven to result from a mutation in any gene," he wrote in a commentary in Nature Genetics.
"With two reports appearing this week from the same laboratory, this Grail of obesity research has now been found-- twice!"
The findings vindicated an approach that stressed biology over willpower and which considered the possibility that some people were more prone to put on fat, no matter what they ate, he said.
